translations.text: Accounts of Events
Further accounts of events, set out briefly.
In the year 513, during the reign of Severus and the reign of King Abgar, son of King Ma‘nu, in the month of November,
the spring of water that flowed from the great palace which King Abgar had built grew strong. It swelled and rose as it had done before.
It filled up and overflowed in every direction. The courtyards, porticoes, and royal buildings began to fill with water. When our lord King Abgar saw this,
he went up to the raised ground on the hill above his palace, where those who did the work of the kingdom lived and stayed.
While the wise men were considering what to do about the excess water that had accumulated, a great and violent rain fell during the night.
The Daisan rose on a day and in a month when it did not normally do so. Water came from elsewhere,
and found the sluice gates closed with large iron plates laid across them and secured with iron bolts.
Since the water could find no entrance, a great lake formed outside the city walls. Water began to descend into the city between the battlements of the wall.
King Abgar, standing in the great tower called the Tower of the Persians, saw the water by the light of flaming torches.
He gave orders, and the gates and the eight sluice gates in the city's western wall, where the river flowed out, were removed.
At that very moment, the water broke through the city's western wall and entered the city.
It swept away the great and splendid palace of our lord the king and carried off everything it found in its path:
the city's lovely and splendid buildings, everything close to the river on its southern and northern sides.
It also damaged the sanctuary of the Christians' church. More than two thousand people died in this disaster.
Many of them were sleeping at night when the water suddenly came upon them, and they drowned.
While the city was filled with the sound of wailing, and when King Abgar saw the destruction that had occurred,
he ordered all the city's craftsmen to move their shops away from the river, and that no one by the river
was to build himself a shop. With the expertise of surveyors and knowledgeable men, the shops were positioned according to the width the river was to have.
They increased its former dimensions. For although the water had been abundant and powerful,
the river's width was also small, since it received the combined waters of twenty-five streams from every direction.
King Abgar also ordered that all those who occupied the portico and worked facing the river
should not spend the night in their shops from October until April. As for the soldiers guarding the city,
five of them were to spend the night on the wall above the place where the water entered the city, throughout the winter.
And when they became aware at night and heard the sound of waters from outside beginning to enter the city.
And anyone who hears the sound but neglects it and does not come out—the waters will hold him accountable for the contempt with which he disregarded the king’s command.
This command was established from the time when this happened, to remain in force forever. Now our lord, King Abgar,
had given orders, and a building was built for him as his royal residence, a winter house at Beth Tabara. He lived there throughout the winter.
In summer he would go down to the new palace that had been built for him at the head of the spring. His nobles also
built themselves houses to live in, in the neighborhood where the king resided, on the upper street called Beth[?] Sahraye.
To restore the city’s former peace, King Abgar gave orders, and the outstanding tax debts of the city’s inhabitants were forgiven,
as were those of the people living in the villages and rural estates. Tax collection from them was suspended for five years, until the city grew rich in population and was adorned with its buildings.
Mar Yahb son of Shamash and Qayuma son of Magartat, the scribes of Edessa, recorded this event and King Abgar’s command.
Bardin and Bolides, who were in charge of the archives of Edessa, received the record and deposited it in the archives as the city’s trusted officials.
In the year 180, kings began to rule in Edessa.
In the year 266, Augustus Caesar became emperor.
In the year 309, our Lord was born.
In the year 400, King Abgar built a funerary monument in honor of his death.
In the year 449, Marcion left the catholic Church.
Lucius Caesar, together with his brother, subjected the Parthians to the Romans in the fifth year of his reign.
In the year 465, on the eleventh day of the month of Tammuz, Bardaisan was born.
In the year 517, Abgar built fortresses in his city.
In the year 551, Mani was born.
In the year 614, the walls of Edessa were breached twice, in the days of Emperor Diocletian.
In the year 624, Bishop Qona laid the foundations of the church of Edessa. Bishop Saad, who succeeded him, built and completed the building.
In the year 635, the cemetery of Edessa was built in the days of Bishop Aithallaha, one year before the great council was held at Nicaea.
In the year 636, Aithallaha became bishop in Edessa. He built the cemetery and the eastern side of the church.
The following year, the council of 318 bishops assembled at Nicaea.
In the year 639, building work and an extension were carried out at the church of Edessa.
In the year 649, Saint Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, died.
In the year 657, Abraham became bishop of Edessa. He built the church of the confessors.
In the year [?] and sixty, Constantius, son of Constantine, built the city of Amida.
And in the year 661, the same Constantius also built the city of Tella, which had formerly been called Antipolis.
In the year 667, Abraham of Qidun became a recluse.
In the year 672, Saint Abraham, bishop of Edessa, departed this world.
And in the same year, Vologeses, bishop of Nisibis, departed this world.
And in the same year, Bishop Barses came from Harran to Edessa by order of the emperor.
In the year 670, Nicomedia was destroyed.
And in the year 674, in the month of June, Julian went down and fought against the Persians, and died there.
In the year 675, in the month of February, Valentinian the Great and his brother Valens became emperors.
In the year 678, Saint Julian the Elder departed this world.
In the year 681, the great baptistery of Edessa was built.
In the year 684, on the ninth day of the month of June, Saint Ephrem [?] departed this world.
And in the month of September of that year, the people left the church of Edessa because of the persecution by the Arians.
In the year 689, in the month of March, Saint Barses, bishop of Edessa, departed this world.
And on the twenty-seventh day of the month of December of that year, the orthodox entered and took possession of the church of Edessa.

And in those days Saint Eulogius became bishop, in the year in which Theodosius the Great became emperor. This Saint Eulogius built the church of Saint Daniel, which was called the church of Saint Dometius.
In the year 692, Theodosius the Great built the city of Reshaina in Azrina[?].
In the year 693, a council of 150 bishops assembled in Constantinople.
In the year 698, Saint Eulogius the bishop departed this world on Good Friday.
In the year 705, on the twenty-second day of the month of August.
They brought the coffin of Saint Thomas the Apostle into his great church, in the days of Bishop Saint Cyrus.
In the year 706, on the seventeenth of January, the great emperor Theodosius departed this world.
And on the twenty-seventh of April, Arcadius entered Constantinople. And on the eighth of November, the body of Theodosius was brought into Constantinople.
And in July of that year, the Huns crossed into Roman territory.
In the year 707, on July 22, Mar Cyrus, bishop of Edessa, departed this world.
And in the year 708, Mar Silvanus became bishop of Edessa.
In the year 710, on October 17, Mar Silvanus, bishop of Edessa, departed this world.
And on November 23 of that year, Mar Pacida became bishop of Edessa.
And in that same year, John Chrysostom became bishop of Constantinople.
In the year 714, Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, began to interpret the Scriptures.
In the year 715, the priest Absamia, the son of the blessed Mar Ephraem’s sister, composed hymns and discourses about the coming of the Huns into Roman territory.
In the year 720, Mar Diogenes became bishop of Edessa. He began to build the church of Mar Barlaha.
And in that same year, on the first day of August, Mar Pacida, bishop of Edessa, departed this world.
In the year 721, Cyril became bishop of Alexandria the Great.
In the year 723, Rabbula became bishop of Edessa. He built the church of Saint Stephen.
It had formerly been a Jewish synagogue. He built it by the emperor’s command.
In the year 724, the walls of Edessa were again breached by floodwater, for the third time, in the days of the victorious emperors Honorius and Arcadius.
In the year 732, the monk Eutyches arose, the one who denied the incarnation.
At this time, the blessed James Intercisus was martyred.
In the year 739, the heresy of those who say that sin is implanted in nature became known.
In the year 740, Andrew, bishop of Samosata, was becoming known.
In the year 741, dust fell from the sky.
In the year 744, the first council assembled at Ephesus.
In the year 746, Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, departed this world on August 8.
The great Ibas succeeded him. He built the new church, which today is called the Church of the Apostles.
In the year 749, in the days of the excellent Ibas.
Senator brought a large silver table weighing 720 pounds, and it was placed in the old church of Edessa.
In the year 753, Anatolius, the military commander, made a silver shrine to honor the bones of the holy apostle Thomas.
In the year 756, Dioscorus became bishop of Alexandria the Great.
Another council was again assembled at Ephesus. It anathematized the great Flavian, bishop of Constantinople,
and Domnus of Antioch, Irenaeus of Tyre, Ibas of Edessa, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, Daniel of Harran, Sophronius of Tella, and Theodoret of Cyrrhus.
In the year 759, Bishop Ibas left Edessa on the first day of January.
On the twenty-first day of July, Nonnus came in his place and remained for two years. He built a sanctuary in the church.
In the year 760, Leo became bishop of Rome.
In the year 762, a council assembled in the city of Chalcedon.
In the year 763, Mar Isaac, the writer and abbot, was well known.
In the year 769, on the twenty-eighth day of October, Ibas, bishop of Edessa, died.
Nonnus came in his place. He built the church of Saint John the Baptist and the hospital for poor lepers outside the Beth-Shemesh Gate.
Within this hospital for the poor, he built a martyrs’ shrine for Saint Cosmas and Saint Damian. He also built monasteries and towers, constructed bridges, and made the roads safe.
In the year 771, the blessed Simeon the Stylite departed this world on the second of September, a Wednesday, at the eleventh hour.
In the year 777, Leo built Callinicum in Osrhoene and named it Leontopolis after himself. He also appointed a bishop there.
In the year 782, Nonnus, bishop of Edessa, died, and Cyrus succeeded him.
In the year 795, Leontius rebelled against Zeno and reigned in Antioch for two years.
In the year 800, the school of the Persians was uprooted from Edessa.
In the year 809, in the month of May, the gold tax was remitted for craftsmen throughout the whole land.
On the sixth day of June, Cyrus, bishop of Edessa, died. Peter succeeded him and entered Edessa on the twelfth of September of that same year.
In the year 810, a great swarm of locusts appeared. It did not do much damage that year, but it did lay eggs.
There was a great earthquake. The hot spring of Dabarhana stopped flowing for [three] days, and the city of Nicopolis was overturned.
It buried all its inhabitants within it, except for the church, the bishop, and two of his attendants.
A sign resembling a lance appeared in the sky for many days during the month of January.
Emperor Anastasius removed Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople, from his position, and Macedonius succeeded him.
In the year 811, a great swarm of locusts came, caused destruction, and devoured all the grain.
In the year 813 [?], on the twenty-second of August, a great fire appeared in the northern region, blazing throughout the night.
In the year 814, Kavadh, king of the Persians, encamped against Amida, a city in Mesopotamia, on October 5. He fought against it and captured it after ninety-seven days.
In September of that same year, he came and encamped against Edessa.
By the grace of God, he caused no damage except that he burned the church of Saint Sergius and the northern basilica of the shrine of the Confessors.
In the year 821, Peter, bishop of Edessa, passed away on Holy Saturday. Paul succeeded him.
In the twenty-first year of his reign, Anastasius ordered that the coffin of Euphemia the martyr be opened,
and that they take out the document that the council assembled at Chalcedon had placed there and burn it.
Fire came out from there and struck the faces of those who wanted to take it out. Because of this, Anastasius abandoned his attempt to take it out of there and burn it.
He did, however, remove Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, because he would not anathematize the council. Timothy succeeded him.
In the twenty-fourth year of Anastasius, Vitalian rebelled against him.
In the year 829, on July 9, Emperor Anastasius departed this world, and Justin succeeded him.
In the second year of Justin's reign, which was the year 830, he expelled Severus from Antioch and Xenaias from Mabbug, along with everyone who would not accept the four councils.
In the year 831, Patricius came to Edessa to remove Paul.
On November 4, he was pressing him to do one of two things: either accept the council and remain on his episcopal throne,
or, if he would not agree, he would remove him from his throne. But Paul would not agree to do either of these things.
Instead, he fled and took refuge in the baptistery. When Patricius saw that he would not agree to do either of these things, and since the emperor's command was fearsome,
he felt compelled to take him out of the baptistery and bring him to Seleucia. When the emperor heard that he had taken him out of the baptistery,
he ordered that he be returned to his throne, in the hope that he would change his mind and accept the council. Paul returned to his throne after forty-four days.
He remained in Edessa for a long time without accepting the council. When the emperor saw that he would not agree, he sent him away to Euchaita.
Paul left Edessa on July 27 in the year 833, and Asclepius succeeded him.
He entered Edessa on October 23 in the year 834, three months after Bishop Paul had left Edessa.
On December 24, after Bishop Asclepius had entered Edessa, he expelled the monks of the Easterners,
both them and all their fellow monks who shared their views, because they would not assent to the Council of Chalcedon.
In the year 836, a great flood entered Edessa for the fourth time. The waters breached its walls, swept away its dwellings, drowned its children, and caused great destruction in it.
For this reason, Bishop Asclepius fled Edessa and went up to the city of Antioch,
to Patriarch Euphrasius. He stayed there for about seventy days, more or less, and died there in Antioch.
On the twenty-seventh of June of that year. And he was buried there in Antioch.
On the fourth of September of that year, they brought his body from Antioch and buried him in the church of Saint Barlaam, above Bishop Nonnus.
When Paul heard that Asclepius had died, he repented and presented a petition to the patrician Justinian. He also drew up a written declaration for Patriarch Euphrasius.
Because of the written declaration he had drawn up, and because of the letter of the illustrious and God-loving patrician Justinian, he was restored and returned to his see.
He entered Edessa on the eighth of March in the year 837, eight months after the death of Asclepius.
After returning to his see, Bishop Paul lived for a period of three [?] and eight months, less eight days. On the thirtieth of October in the year 838, Bishop Paul passed away.
Andrew succeeded him and entered Edessa on the seventh of February of that year, the year 838.
The God-loving Emperor Justinian devoted care and attention to the matter until he entered the four holy councils in the church's diptychs.
These were the council of Nicaea, that of Constantinople, the first council at Ephesus, and that of Chalcedon.
In the thirteenth year of Justinian's reign, which was the year 850, in the second indiction.
A sign resembling a spear appeared in the sky on the fifth of October.
In the year 837, on the twenty-ninth of May, on Friday at the seventh hour, there was a great and violent earthquake.
Much of Antioch collapsed in it, crushing its children and suffocating its inhabitants.
In the year 839, on the fifteenth of November, there was a great fire in Antioch.
It burned much of what had survived the earthquake. It was not known where the fire had started.
Patriarch Euphrasius also died in this earthquake and was buried beneath the rubble. As people say, he kept crying out from beneath the rubble all day.
After him, Ephraim of Amida became bishop there in Antioch. He had been Count of the East.
In the year 844, on the sixth of December, Bishop Andrew departed this world.
He was laid in the church of Saint Barlaam, above the bones of Nonnus and Asclepius. Addai succeeded him.
He entered Edessa on the twenty-eighth of August [?] in the year 844.
In the year 838, on the first day of April, Justinian became Caesar. And on the tenth of April.
Justinian became Caesar. On the tenth of August of that year, Emperor Justinian passed away, and Justinian reigned alone.
In the year 842, in July, Demosthenes came down to Edessa to take command of the Roman forces.
In December of the year 843, on the eighteenth of the month, the Huns entered Roman territory.
They took captives and laid waste as far as the territory of Aleppo, and [?] to the Dodecaton of Antioch.
And because of this distress, Lord Demosthenes fell ill and died in the city of Tella, on January 10 of that year.
And in the year 843, in September of that year, peace—peace between the Persians and the Romans—was made
by Lord Rufinus, the patrician. This peace lasted until the year 851.
And in this same year, in the month of [?] eight hundred and fifty-one. And in this same year, in May, Khosrow, king of the Persians, broke the peace.
He crossed into Roman territory and devastated Sura, Aleppo, and Antioch. He also took control of Apamea. Then he turned back and came as far as Edessa.
But by the grace of God, its protector, he did it no harm. Instead, the city's leaders paid him, and he took two hundred pounds of gold and returned to his own country.
As we have learned from earlier histories, the waters have now breached the walls of the blessed city four times, knocked down its towers,
and swept away its children, since Christ ascended to his glorious Father. The first time its walls were breached was in the days of Severus, emperor of the Romans,
in the year 513 according to the reckoning of the Greeks, in November.
The second time its walls were breached again was in the days of Emperor Diocletian, in the year 614, in May.
The third time its walls were breached again was in the days of the victorious emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year 724, in March,
on the eighteenth of that month, on Tuesday, when it was [?]. They were breached again in the days of Emperor Justin,
in the year 836, when Asclepius was bishop in Edessa.
